items.html:
Best GPU opportunity is repeated sampling/illumination with fixed geometry, followed by a new resident matrix-free cluster path. The old branch does not justify making GPU dense LU the default.

All branch citations below refer to preserved commit 51d2f1c18a4941c39f0b33dacbc1883bf1be470e. Local Git reports 40 commits exclusive to current main and one exclusive to the experimental branch since their common ancestor. The branch was isolated deliberately, rather than abandoned because every GPU path failed.

Historical workload, RTX 4080 SUPER vs Ryzen 9950X Recorded result What it establishes
Cached plane-field sampling, 16,384 points × 512 modes Rust 7.12×; Python 6.43× Strong warm throughput opportunity
Cached sampling, 32,768 × 1,024 Rust 7.74×; Python 7.49× Same, with 1.5 GiB cached operator
Fused plane field, 64–1,024 modes 1.53–2.77× Useful, modest, avoids huge cached operator
Complex128 LU + 64 RHS, dimension 4,096, host round trip 1.14× Near parity
Reused LU, same shape, resident 0.82× GPU slower despite retention
Resident matrix action, 4,096 × 64 RHS 2.02× Shape-specific gain; wider 2,048 × 512 case was 0.71×

Evidence: sampling timings and baseline selection, fused field timings, dense timings.

Important boundaries:

  • Cached sampling preserves complex128, includes coefficient upload and field download, and compares with CPU reuse and a prepared fused CPU alternative, across CPU thread counts. But cold Python setup required approximately 138/86 applications to break even, and the matrices consumed 384 MiB/1.5 GiB. Those break-even figures are estimates from setup and warm measurements, not measured optimization-loop totals. (Source)
  • The reported 9.49–10.81× coefficient-adjoint gain is versus cached CPU matrix products only. A prepared fused CPU adjoint was not measured. The GPU path has no wavevector/geometry derivatives or automatic JAX/PyTorch/Advect integration. (Source)
  • These are September historical measurements against the old core, not current-main performance claims. Main’s spherical-field improvements do not directly invalidate plane-field results: the old plane forward loop already resembles current pw/field.rs:247. Current parallel scheduling and gradient implementation still require fresh comparisons.

What I would revive:

  1. Port the small resident complex128 matrix backend and its numerical tests onto main. The branch already implements retained device matrices, cuBLAS Hermitian products, pivoted cuSOLVER LU, shared CPU equilibration, and an implicit solve pullback. Reuse this rather than writing dense algebra kernels. (Backend implementation), resident solve/pullback
  2. Use that to test complete repeated-illumination/objective loops. Keep operator, vectors, field cotangents and reductions resident when the workflow permits. Measure cold setup, warm iteration and total optimization time separately. The branch’s strongest demonstrated acceleration is here.
  3. Try a smaller, exact sampling representation before cementing the old cache design. For plane waves, write (E=S W), where (S_{pm}=\exp(i k_m\cdot r_p)) and (W_{mj}=c_m e_{mj}). Cache one scalar phase matrix instead of three field components. This cuts operator storage exactly 3×: 384→128 MiB and 1.5 GiB→512 MiB. A three-column product may also reuse phase loads; actual runtime gain is unmeasured. CPU receives the same optimization. The factorization follows directly from the implemented field equation.
  4. Keep the fused cuTile kernel as a qualified experiment, not the first new optimization project. It already eliminates the point×mode matrix and supports lossy/evanescent waves, but still loops over modes for each point tile, calls f64 trigonometry, and always returns results to the host. It has no GPU pullback. Its own probes found only ~4 ms transfer cost within a roughly 60–70 ms large evaluation, so removing transfers alone will not produce a dramatic forward speedup. (Kernel), profile

Matrix-free GPU is substantial new work, not branch revival. Main currently recomputes a translation block for every particle pair on every operator application, then immediately contracts it; GMRES solves RHS columns sequentially. A GPU implementation should retain mode/translation-plan data, particle geometry, Mie blocks, Krylov vectors and reductions on device, and fuse pair generation with contraction. A host GMRES loop repeatedly uploading vectors would retain too much synchronization and launch overhead. Forward and adjoint actions plus pairwise geometry-gradient contractions must be implemented together. Current reference paths: pair action, GMRES orchestration, adjoint and gradients. The branch’s physical cluster test merely assembles the operator/RHS on CPU and sends the dense solve to GPU; it is not GPU scattering assembly. (Test)

Matrix-free acceleration may have greater eventual impact for large low-order particle systems with few illuminations, but still has quadratic pair work and depends on convergence/preconditioning. A GPU does not remove either limitation.

Do not conclude that H100-class hardware is unpromising from the RTX result. NVIDIA documents only two native f64 arithmetic results/cycle/SM for compute capability 8.9 versus 64 for 9.0; actual application scaling remains unmeasured. Testing the existing dense benchmark once on a GPU designed for FP64 is a cheaper discriminator than rewriting LU. NVIDIA instruction-throughput table, H100 specifications

A selective port is required: plane became pw; equilibrate and its scale type became crate-private; NumPy conversion helpers moved; CUDA PyO3 methods lack today’s mandatory fpenv::ieee wrappers; old benchmarks use global Rayon/faer parallelism. See current equilibration boundary, current conversion ownership, old binding. Restore selected backend code/tests against current numerical conventions; do not merge the old CPU implementation wholesale.

Verified read-only source/history and historical qualification records. No checkout, edits, fetch, GPU runs or new measurements; nothing pushed or posted.
